### Downloads

| file | for |
|---|---|
| `aht-<version>-macos-universal.zip` | macOS 13+, Apple Silicon and Intel (`aht.app`: menu bar tray + core + watcher + badge tool) |
| `aht-setup-<version>-windows-x64.exe` | **Windows 11 on x64: the installer** (for you only, no admin prompt; Start menu entry, Settings > Apps to remove it) |
| `aht-setup-<version>-windows-arm64.exe` | Windows 11 on ARM: the installer (native build) |
| `aht-<version>-windows-x64.zip` | Windows 11 on x64 without installing (`aht.exe`, `aht-tray.exe` and their `_internal` folder; run `aht install`) |
| `aht-<version>-windows-arm64.zip` | the same for Windows 11 on ARM |
| `SHA256SUMS.txt` | checksums of the above |

Package managers: `brew install --cask havurgiray/tap/aht` (macOS), `winget install havurgiray.aht` (Windows, the installer above), `scoop install aht` (Windows, after adding the `havurgiray/scoop-bucket` bucket). Linux installs from the checkout (`linux/install.sh`).

**Windows, if you used aht before 0.14.0:** Windows Security took the small script older versions started the watcher with at sign-in for malware and removed it, so the watcher may not have started at sign-in since.  0.14.0 starts it without any script; run the installer, or `aht install` once, to set it up again.

**Scoop:** run `aht install` once after `scoop update aht` to 0.14.0.  The hook and the sign-in entry then go through Scoop's `current` folder, so they keep working after later updates.

**Mac, a path with `&` or `<`:** a watched folder, a home folder or an app location whose path holds `&` or `<` now gives valid LaunchAgents (the watcher, the notices, start at login).  Before, launchd would not load them, so the watcher silently did not run.  After the upgrade, Settings > This Mac > *Reinstall or Update aht…* rewrites them (`aht install` in a terminal rewrites the watcher's and the notices').

**Privacy: keys are masked whole.** Fixes to the masking in 0.13.0 and earlier: a key, token or password that aht recognises in an agent's history is now masked whole, however long (up to 64 KB), and before the text is shortened, wherever aht copies text out of a history: the search index (messages, the commands, file paths and web addresses of tool calls, and session titles), handover and switch summaries, the journal, notices (also on the phone), shared session pages (also `--tools`), Tidy Up's preview, What Changed, and the notes for informed sessions, loose ends and second opinions.  Session titles and names, tab titles and names waiting for a session's next prompt are now masked wherever aht lists them: the session board (also what other machines receive, and other machines'), loose ends, a handover's dry run and result, Take Back, What Changed, `aht undo --list`, `aht checkup` (also its `--restart` plan), `aht sessions`, `aht tab-names` (its list, `--json` and its sync plan), saved workspaces, and `aht limits`' usage-limit text.  They stay as they are only on this computer: in the Mac's session corner, the iTerm2 tab titles aht sets, aht's files about tabs in `~/.aht/run`, the tab titles of saved workspaces (restoring a layout sets them back) and `aht.log`.  Earlier versions could leave part of a long key in clear (for example most of an API key after `x-api-key:`, or a long Google, Firebase or Azure ID token), could cut a text, such as a tool's command at 400 characters, in the middle of a key before masking it, masked only the first line of a private key (and masked the BEGIN line of a guide that only named one), cut a password in quotes at a `,`, `;` or closing bracket in it, took a value of capital letters and digits (a TOTP seed, say), a dotted value or one starting with `/`, `~` or `.` for a name or a path, and missed `Authorization: Bearer` tokens.  Now also masked: values after names that contain a secret word (`DB_PASSWORD=`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=`, `SECRET_KEY=`, `JWT_SECRET=`, `client_secret`, `GITHUB_TOKEN=`, `PGPASSWORD=`, `x-api-key:`, `RAILS_MASTER_KEY=`, `APP_KEY=`, `*_PAT=`, `passphrase`, in a `.env` file or an `export` line too) and after camelCase and PascalCase names (`dbPassword`, `accessToken`, `SecretAccessKey`, `SessionToken`), but not names that say they hold something else (`TOKEN_URL`, `password_hash`, `token_type`, `max_tokens`, `accessTokenUrl`) or a page's token (`NextToken`, `nextPageToken`); a value in quotes, over the `,`, `;` and brackets in it; `Authorization:` with any scheme, and `Basic` credentials; passwords and tokens on a command line (`--password`, `--token`, `--with-token`, `--api-key` and the like, `mysql -p`, `docker login -p`, `twine -p`, `sshpass -p`, `redis-cli -a`, `curl -u user:password`), and in XML (`<password>…</password>`, `key="…Password" value="…"`); Google OAuth tokens (`ya29.…`), GitLab, SendGrid, PyPI, age, Vault, DigitalOcean, Shopify, Docker Hub and Atlassian tokens, the secret part of Slack webhook addresses and Telegram bot tokens; passwords in database addresses whatever the host (`localhost`, an IP address, a container's name such as `@db`, `[::1]`), with or without a user name, also percent-encoded or with an `@` in them, and in Go's form `user:password@tcp(…)`, with the rest of the address left readable; passwords with symbols in them (`$`, `%`, `(`, `{`, a closing bracket), masked whole; tokens followed by `...`, `</code>` or `%0A`; passwords of 12 to 16 characters that mix three kinds of character (small and capital letters, digits, symbols); and private keys from their BEGIN line to their END line (also with `>` or `#` before each line), also inside JSON (and JSON inside JSON), in Read-tool output with line numbers, encrypted keys with `Proc-Type` and `DEK-Info` lines, PGP private-key blocks, PuTTY `.ppk` files, and keys in base64 (a kubeconfig's `client-key-data`, a Kubernetes `tls.key`).  Left alone: ordinary code that uses the words token, password, secret or auth (`token = tokenizer.encode(text)`, `password: Optional[str]`), placeholders and references to a secret store (`${DB_PASSWORD}`, `op://…`, `vault:…`), test names, paths, hashes and words, and a guide or code that names a private key's BEGIN and END lines.  Masking is best effort: aht cannot recognise every secret, and aht does not try to guess at every shape a secret could have; PRIVACY.md lists the known limits (a value with no name or form it knows, one that does not look generated, a password with a quote or a space in it, a private key seen only from its middle, among others), so keep secrets out of agent chats.  On a large history, finding keys now takes about 1.5 times as long as in 0.13.0.  Journals and summaries written before stay as they were.

**The search index is rebuilt once**, by itself, at its first update after this version: an index from an earlier version could hold parts of keys, for example from long tool commands.  The old file is deleted first, so the rebuild needs no extra disk space and nothing of its old rows stays (on Windows, while a search has the file open, its tables are emptied and the file compacted instead), so `aht search --rebuild` by hand is not needed.  While an update runs, the watcher and the session-start hook no longer start more updates that would only wait for it.  A session whose history file is gone and that no history backup holds is no longer searchable after that rebuild.

**`aht secrets`** now also lists `Bearer` and `Basic` credentials, `.env` names, connection strings and the other forms above, also a name at the start of a later line of a tool's output and in JSON inside JSON (before, `aht secrets`, `--redact` and the handover's count found such a name only on the first line), so it may list more finds than before, and fewer false ones in code.  It lists a private key once, as its header, even when the history holds it twice (the Read tool's numbered copy and the file's text), and `--redact` takes out the key from its BEGIN line to its END line, and nothing around it (0.13.0 took out only the header line); a place whose removal would leave a line of the history no longer valid JSON is left as it is, and aht says so; a header with no key under it, as in a guide, is no longer listed.  A new scan then no longer finds it.  A key of a known kind is listed once, not again as *password or token*.

**Linux:** the watcher's systemd unit now really applies its start limit: when the watcher keeps crashing and is started 5 times within 60 seconds, systemd stops restarting it, instead of trying every 10 seconds forever.  A restart you ask for (Restart Watcher, adding or removing a watched folder, `aht roots`, `aht reload`, setup, or resuming in the tray) clears that limit first: it never stops the watcher, and it starts a stopped one again at once.  `linux/install.sh` (or `aht reload`) rewrites the unit.  Start-at-login entries now also work for folder names with a newline or tab, and when the path to Python holds a `%` they start the same Python by a path without one.

**Linux, git folders:** the git mark is now aht's own emblem, a white disc with a dark "+", instead of the theme's link arrow, which made git folders look like links.  After the update the watcher puts it on every git folder once; `linux_git_emblem` still picks another emblem.  `aht uninstall --remove-icons` now also removes the emblem images aht drew, and `~/.local/share/icons/hicolor/icon-theme.cache` when aht's emblems were the last icons there; when other icons remain, it writes that cache again without aht's emblems.

**Windows, folder badges:** aht no longer keeps a badge it had to draw without Windows' own folder icon (for example the flat ∞ folder an older aht cached).  A folder whose badge shows such a plain drawn folder gets Windows' own on its next refresh (`aht icons --refresh`, or *Refresh all badges* in the tray) or its next badge change.  aht removes older versions' cache files in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\aht\icons` the first time it makes a badge.  A folder's badge in Explorer now also changes as soon as aht changes it, including after `aht icons --refresh`, even in an Explorer window that is already open: the badge file is now `.aht\aht-badge-<8 hex>.ico`, named after its picture, so Explorer draws a changed one afresh, and the old file goes.

**Removing a history** (`aht tidy --remove-history`, and *Remove…* in the Mac app's Tidy Up): on Windows a history now goes to the Recycle Bin, and only there.  When it cannot (the drive has no Recycle Bin, its bin removes files at once, or the history is bigger than the bin holds), aht changes nothing and says why; you can still delete it yourself.  A link in Claude's history folder (to a folder elsewhere) is listed but never removed: the Mac app's Tidy Up shows it as *Claude Code, a link to a folder elsewhere*, without *Remove…*.  A refused removal prints the name and why, never what it would have done.

**Options given twice** now add up: `aht setup --apply --adopt A --adopt B` takes on both, and `aht config --set backup_keep=20 --set notify_finished=false` sets both.  Before, only the last one counted.

**Choosing a folder in aht's window** (Windows and Linux): *Cancel* just closes the chooser.  On Windows you can type or paste a path into the chooser's *Folder:* field; a path with no folder behind it is reported, and nothing changes.  The Windows chooser no longer goes through PowerShell, which compiled a few lines of C# each time (a pattern antivirus tools often flag): aht shows Windows' own folder dialog itself, in a second process (`aht.exe _pick-folder`).

**New projects:** the *A new project is found* setting is gone.  aht takes on new projects as you work in them; an old config's `new_policy` and `--news` from old scripts are accepted and ignored.  A project you *Forget* now stays forgotten: the next scan does not take it on again, and setting up again lists it unticked.  It comes back when you take it on yourself: a new Claude Code session in its folder, `aht tag`, *Adopt This Mac's Projects…* or `aht adopt`, ticking it when you set up again, Tidy Up's *Reconnect* or *Choose Folder…* onto it (`aht bind`), `aht restore` into it, handing it over or keeping it in sync.  The adopt question names up to three such folders, then "and N more", in the Mac app and in the trays.

**Five agents, and Hand Back:** Switch Agent now also offers Antigravity (the `agy` command) and Mistral Vibe (the `vibe` command), next to Claude Code, Codex and Kimi Code; the menu lists the ones installed.  The agent that takes over goes on in a new session that reads a summary of where things stood, or in its own latest session in the project, which reads only a catch-up of what happened since (`aht switch <path> --to X --resume`).  *Summary Only* (`--brief-only`) writes the summary and opens nothing; who has the project stays as it was.  While another agent has a project, a line under it says so (*Codex has had this project since 14:10, taken over from Claude Code*), with *Hand Back…*, also the first item under Switch Agent: the first agent's own session opens again and reads what happened meanwhile: the other agents' exchanges, the to-dos still open, the files changed (from git) and the commits made (`aht switch <path> --back`).  When that session is gone, a new one reads the full summary and the catch-up; when aht cannot read what the other agent did, the catch-up says the files may differ all the same.  Hand Back to Claude Code, or going on in Claude Code's own session, costs no tokens until you type: aht's hook gives the session its catch-up as it opens.  Switching to, or handing back to, Codex, Kimi Code, Antigravity or Mistral Vibe is one turn of that agent; writing a summary costs nothing.  A Claude session that another agent took the work over from, resumed by hand, is told in one line that the files may have changed and where the summary is.  Each hand-off leaves a record next to its summary in the project's `.aht/handover/`, and `aht relays <path>` lists who handed the work to whom and when.  Summaries now also hold the state of git, the files a Codex patch changed and Codex's plan, and say how many Codex sessions aht cannot read (Codex's newer storage).  aht reads the sessions of Codex 0.164, which keeps them in a new format, as well as older ones; Codex's background service no longer counts as an open Codex session.  Kimi Code goes on in its own session too; when Kimi does not take the catch-up there, a new session reads the full summary, and aht says so.  aht reads Antigravity's conversations too, so it can continue one and catch it up; and Mistral Vibe's sessions (those of Vibe 3) the same way, in search, summaries and catch-ups as well, without ever changing them.

**Handovers that were cut off:** when the link drops or the computer sleeps during a handover, aht now finds out at its next check whether the session on the other machine started, and finishes the handover or undoes it: "Handover of api to box finished: the session there runs (the link had dropped at 01:02)", or "The handover of api to box did not finish. The project stays here; nothing runs there".  It counts as finished whenever something happened there: a session runs there, the copy there changed, "the conversation went on there", or "the session there started, and has ended since"; "did not finish" only when nothing happened there, so work done there is never dropped.  Folders taken along with `--include` come back at Take Back here too.  A handover that fails before the session starts says "did not finish" at once.  The Mac app and aht's window show such a project with *Check Now*, which asks the other machine at once, and *Release…*; until it is settled, Continue Session, Switch Agent, Hand Over and Keep in sync wait.  The Mac menu lists such projects, and a click on the notice opens the project.  A session started in the project meanwhile is warned.  On Linux the tray shows these notices, and with `notify_phone` they reach the phone too.

**Release:** `aht reclaim <path> --release` (dry run first, then `--apply`) lets a project count as here again when the other machine is gone or does not answer: the files here stay as they are, the copy there is left alone, and the work done there stays there ("The work done on box since 14:10 stays on box. It does not come here. What stays there: 3 files and the conversation.").  It says nothing stays behind only when neither the files nor the conversation changed there.  When the project is kept in sync with that machine, Release pauses Keep in sync, so no sync overwrites the copy left there (the dry run says "Keep in sync with box will be paused, so the copy there stays as it is", the result "Keep in sync with box is paused, so the copy there stays as it is"); it stays paused until you turn it back on (*Turn Sync Back On…* in the Mac app and in aht's window, or `aht mirror <path> --on --to box`), or until a later Hand Over to that machine, which sets the released copy aside there first.  It is offered after an hour without an answer.  The Mac app has *Release…* next to *Take Back…* for any handed-over project; aht's window has *More → Release from <machine>…*, named as the machine was added.  `aht remote remove`, and *Remove…* in the Machines tab, now say why a machine that still holds a project is not removed and point to Release.  The next session in a released project is told once that the work done there did not come here.  Take Back now refuses a saved list of what left that belongs to another handover attempt, and points to Release.

**Keep in sync:** a sync run now checks each project again right before it sends it, so a project released, handed over or switched off while the run is under way is not sent (the run lists it as *paused* or *skipped*), so a run under way no longer replaces the copy a Release or a handover just left there.

**Nothing lost on the way back:** a file whose name changed only in case on the other machine (`readme.md` → `README.md`) now comes back on a Mac, with the old one set aside; two names that differ only in case are both kept; empty folders made there (a packed git repo's `refs`) come back too.  Files set aside, here and on the other machine, keep the newest 5 folders and everything younger than 30 days; Claude's checkpoints and plans replaced on the other machine are now set aside too.  A project's `.aht/handover/` keeps every hand-off that is still open and the newest 12 other summaries, handover and switch alike (before, 5 and 8, and each kind deleted the other's).  Keep in sync no longer sends that folder, and a handover never removes anything from it on the other machine.

**Backups on another machine:** each computer now gets a folder of its own there, named by a random id, so two computers of one name no longer share a folder.  Copying only adds: a backup there is removed only after this computer pruned it, and at least 3 per project always stay.  The copies aht makes before it rewrites a history go there too and are never removed there; a fetch brings back the ones missing here.  New: `aht backup --offsite-list` lists every computer's folder there, and `aht backup --fetch-offsite [--from ID|NAME]` fetches from one; a fetch adds what is missing and never overwrites (a same-named backup of another size arrives as `<stamp>-from-<name>.zip`).  An older aht's folder named after this computer is taken over only when everything in it is here too, and goes once nothing is left in it; otherwise it stays, *Copy Now* says so, and *Fetch Backups From…* can bring its backups here.  The Mac app and aht's window (on Linux, and now on Windows too) have Settings → Backups on another machine with *Copy Now* and *Fetch Backups From…*.

**The other machine:** `aht remote add` and `aht remote check` now stop on a Windows PC ("aht cannot ask a Windows machine yet") after one harmless `echo` there and make nothing on it; before, they left folders named `-p` and `$HOME` in the PC's home.  The copy of aht placed on the other machine is now named after its checksum (`~/.aht/remote/aht-<checksum>.py`; the newest 3 stay, the old `aht.py` goes) and is sent only when it is missing, not with every look at that machine's sessions.  What a session waits for is masked before it leaves that machine, and before it reaches the phone.

**A Windows PC asks your other machines:** aht on Windows now adds, checks and watches your Mac and Linux machines over Windows' own ssh, shows their sessions in the Sessions tab and searches them.  A PC is never asked itself, so it needs no ssh server.  *Check* (`aht remote check`) now groups its rows *For asking* and *For handing over*, and on a PC its fixes are Windows' own (ssh-agent, accepting a machine's key once, Remote Login on a Mac).  The guide's new *A Windows PC with your other machines* walks through the keys.

**Watch a machine:** a *Watch* switch for each machine (`aht remote watch <machine> [--off]`): aht asks it every 2 minutes and tells you when a session there waits for you or is done, also when it holds no project of yours.  The Machines tab says when aht last heard from each one.  Once you added a machine, every notice names its machine ("api on box waits for you"), and a notice from another machine reaches the phone only once: not when aht there sends it already.  A machine that holds a project and has not answered for 10 minutes gives one notice ("box has not answered since 15:20. The work on api there may have stopped (asleep, off or offline).").  In Sessions, a machine that does not answer keeps the sessions it had, greyed, "as of 11:40".

**Search everywhere:** *Also on my other machines* in Search (`aht search <words> --everywhere`): each machine searches its own index, read only, and its results come labelled with its name.  aht builds no index there and keeps nothing of the results.

**Pick Up and Leave a Note:** go on with a project's work on another machine, in any agent, and give it back later.  Only the context moves; git moves the files, and each machine keeps its own copy of the project, at any path.  *Machines → Pick Up from box…* (`aht pickup <path> --from box`) brings a summary of the latest session in the project on box, made and masked there, and says what git still has to do ("On box: branch main, 1 commit not pushed, 1 file not committed. Commit and push there, then pull here.").  *Open in* starts the agent you choose with it (one turn: uses tokens); *Copy the Start Line* writes it and opens nothing.  aht finds the project there by its id, else by its git origin and first commit, its path or its place in the home folder, and when two folders could be it, it lists both instead of guessing.  *Leave a Note on box…* (`aht leave-note <path> --on box`) puts a summary of the work here into the project's `.aht/handover/` on box; aht only adds files there, nothing runs there and it costs no tokens.  When the work comes back the way it went, the summary is a catch-up for the session it left, which goes on in its own session; while work picked up from box is here, *Hand Back to box…* leaves such a note there.  A note that arrives gives a notice, a line under the project with *Read the Note…*, and one line to the next Claude session there.  A Windows PC starts every exchange: Pick Up from the Mac, then Leave a Note on it before you go.  In Search, a result from another machine offers *Continue Here…*, which picks that session up here.

**Keep in sync looks before it overwrites:** before each sync aht compares the copy on the other machine with its list from the last sync, handover or take-back, so no clock matters.  When that copy was worked on (a file that was only touched does not count), when the sync would remove more than 200 files there or more than a quarter of at least 20, or when a first sync would go into a folder that holds something else, the sync pauses, sends nothing and gives one notice ("Keep in sync paused: api").  The project lists the files and offers *Bring Them Here…* (Take Back on the copy: a file changed on both machines keeps both versions, then the sync runs; `aht reclaim <path> --apply`), *Replace Them…* (`aht mirror <path> --replace --apply`; theirs are set aside there), *Allow the Removals…* (`--allow-removals --apply`) or *Stop Syncing* (`--off`).  Hand Over now stops over a changed copy too; `aht handover <path> --replace-there` sets that work aside there and goes on.  Turning a released sync back on looks first in the same way.  The other machine notes its copies in `~/.aht/remote/copies.json`, so aht there refuses to keep such a folder in sync as well, *Keep All Projects in Sync* there leaves it out, the project there says *Copy kept in sync from mac*, and a Claude session there hears one line about it.  In the Machines tab each machine says how many projects are kept in sync with it and how many are paused.  Names the other disk cannot hold apart (`README.md` and `readme.md`) are listed by `aht mirror --run --json` and by the dry runs of `--replace` and `--allow-removals`.

**aht's own file copy:** files now move between your machines without rsync.  rsync still copies them when this machine has rsync 3, the other has rsync, and neither is Windows; otherwise aht's own copy does, over the same ssh, with nothing but python3 on the other machine.  rsync is now optional: it makes big changes faster.  aht's own copy sends each file in pieces of at most 1 MB, checks it when it has arrived and only then puts it in place (if that fails, the old file goes back); what it replaces or removes is set aside first, on whichever machine receives, as with rsync.  A file that only grew, such as a conversation that went on, sends just its new end.  Against rsync it gives up two things: a big file changed in the middle is sent whole, and a big file cut off halfway starts again next time (the files that arrived whole stay).  The new setting `handover_transfer` (`auto`, `rsync` or `aht`; Settings → Handover → *Copies files with*, in the Mac app and in aht's window) chooses, and *Check* (`aht remote check`) says which one each machine gets.  `aht doctor` now lists rsync 3 as optional.  **From Windows:** a PC now copies its backups to one of your Mac or Linux machines after each daily backup (*Copy Now*, `aht backup --offsite`), and *Fetch Backups From…* (`aht backup --fetch-offsite`) brings backups from there to the PC.  A backup that cannot be put in place is named, the others still arrive, and `aht backup --fetch-offsite` then ends with exit code 1.

**Between Mac, Windows and Linux, at any path:** Hand Over and Take Back now work from a Windows PC too, with your Mac and Linux machines, and a project may sit at another path on each machine.  New: *Bring Here* (`aht bring <path there> --from <machine>`; *Projects → Bring Here → From …*) runs on the machine that gets the work.  It fetches a project with Claude Code's history and opens its session in a terminal, where nothing runs until you type; the project's home notes that it is away.  *Send Back* (`aht send-back <path>`) returns the work: the home plans it as Take Back would, and sets aside what it replaces.  So a PC, which no machine can reach, works on a Mac's project: the Mac shows "On pc since 14:10 (brought there from pc). Send it back from pc." with *Release…*, and the PC's tray lists *Projects brought here* with *Send Back…*.  Both need aht installed on the project's home.  Where projects go is a rule per machine (`aht remote paths <machine> [--same | --home | --add HERE THERE | --remove HERE]`; *Machines → Folders there → Change…* in aht's window): a machine added now gets them at the same place below its home folder, and one set up before keeps the same paths when your home folder's path exists there.  A project outside every rule is refused, with the line that fixes it.  Claude Code's history is filed under the folder's path there; /rewind's snapshots go only on an unchanged path; other agents' histories stay, and the session gets a summary.  Before anything moves, aht refuses a folder there that holds something else, and names the other disk cannot hold (Windows' reserved names and characters, two names that differ only in case, links your account cannot make there), with *Leave Them Out…* (`handover_excludes`).  On the way back, a file that changed only in its line endings is not taken, one whose line endings flipped as a whole gets back the ones it left with, executable marks survive a round trip through a PC, and a file whose name Windows cannot hold is kept aside under a safe name.  A session aht starts gets `core.filemode=false` on a PC (and `core.autocrlf=true` for a project from a PC whose git converts line endings) through `GIT_CONFIG_*` in its environment; `.git/config` is never edited.  For a git project without a `.gitattributes` that crosses to or from Windows, the dry run suggests lines for one, which aht never writes.

**The other machine stays awake:** while the agent works on a project handed over to a Mac or Linux machine, aht keeps that machine from sleeping (`caffeinate`; `systemd-inhibit`, or GNOME's own inhibitor where ssh sessions may not use it; `handover_keep_awake`, on by default).  A closed lid still sleeps.  *Check* says whether it works there.

**Welcome and start at login:** a first setup that turns *start at login* off is now kept as your answer, in the Mac app and in aht's window, so *Getting started* marks the login step optional.

**Privacy policy:** [PRIVACY.md](https://github.com/havurgiray/agent-history-tether/blob/main/PRIVACY.md) changed with this release.  aht can now look for new versions (off until you say yes; GitHub then sees your computer's address and which version you run), reads three of iTerm2's settings for *Getting started*, and on Windows and Linux serves aht's window to your own browser at 127.0.0.1 only.  The policy now also lists what a handover reads and changes in Claude Code's `~/.claude.json`, the copies aht keeps of Claude Code's `settings.json`, the files under `~/.aht/run` and the notices check's log, where a history you remove with `aht tidy` goes on each system, when aht reads `~/.ssh/config` and Tailscale's machine list (to list machines you could add, and to reach one you added), that aht's log records your other machines' names (and a Tailscale address it reached one by), that `registry.json` keeps the identifiers of projects you told aht to forget (and the git repositories and declined moves it already kept), `run/autostart.json`, your answer about starting the tray at login, how aht checks a Windows Recycle Bin before and after it moves a history there, the emblem images aht draws on Linux (and their icon cache), that the window's folder chooser on Windows no longer goes through PowerShell, the new `~/.aht/machine.json` (a random id of this computer, its name and when it was made) and `~/.aht/offsite.json` (which backups went to which machine; it replaces `~/.aht/run/offsite.json`), the folder of this computer's own for backups on another machine and how long backups stay there, how long set-aside files are kept here and there, the handover data in `registry.json`, the `.aht-write-test-…` and `.aht-case-…` files aht briefly makes, that a waiting session's text is masked before it leaves that machine, the handover notices on the phone, Windows' new badge file names, and Kimi Code's real folder (`~/.kimi-code`).  It also says what aht masks and where, that masking is best effort and what its known limits are, where session names and tab titles stay as they are (on this computer only: the session corner, the tab titles aht sets, `run/tab-names.json`, `run/iterm-tabs.json`, saved workspaces' tab titles and `aht.log`), what a shared page masks and removes and what it leaves (paths outside your home folder), that the search index keeps what tool calls worked on and is built anew once after an update from an earlier version, that saved workspaces keep each session's name with keys masked, this computer's name and the options each Claude session was started with, that `registry.json` records when a release paused Keep in sync (why, when and for which machine), that the copies made before a rewrite go to the backup machine too and stay there, and the small files aht writes in `~/.aht/remote/run/` on the other machine to start a handover's session (with when it started).  For switching between agents it now also says what aht reads of Antigravity's (`agy`) data folder (a copy of its summary database, and a conversation's transcript and plan files), and that it will never read its `cli.log`, `history.jsonl`, `implicit/` or `settings.json`; what it reads of Mistral Vibe's (`vibe`) data folder (each session's `meta.json`, and its history from the generation and journal files, never the agent's reasoning), and that it will never read Vibe's `config.toml`, `.env`, `vibehistory`, `trusted_folders.toml`, caches, logs or the model's own context; that a switch reads a copy of Codex's `state_5.sqlite` only to count the sessions it cannot read, and takes a patch's files and the plan from Codex's sessions; what the records of who handed the work to whom in a project's `.aht/handover/` hold (also this computer's name and random id, so the first switch makes `machine.json`); the project's git state a summary reads; that aht looks at which agent programs run (on Windows, before a switch, the names of the running programs); and the line aht's hook adds to a Claude session another agent took the work over from, and a Hand Back's catch-up (also for Claude Code's own session when you switch to it); and that of a hand-off record that came with a project folder aht reads only what it writes there itself.  It now also covers a Windows PC asking your other machines, what aht reads from them when you ask (their open sessions, every 2 minutes for a machine you watch, and search excerpts, masked there), the last session list it keeps in `~/.aht/run/board.json`, that notices name their machine and when they skip the phone, and how aht keeps a machine awake while a handed-over agent works there (with its small `awake.pid` file there).  For Pick Up and Leave a Note it says what aht sends to find the project on the other machine and what it reads there (a session summary and git state, masked there), what it writes into the project's `.aht/handover/` there (only new files, at most 200 KB each), the new `~/.aht/run/incoming.jsonl`, the notices and hook lines for notes that arrived, and Pick Up's *Open in* among the features that start an agent.  For Keep in sync it covers the file lists (and some checksums) aht reads from the copy there before each sync, the lists (and checksums) it keeps per machine in `~/.aht/handover/<project id>/there/`, what a paused sync records in `registry.json`, the new `~/.aht/remote/copies.json` on the other machine (the folder there, the project's id, this computer's name and random id, the kind of copy and since when), the hook's line in such a folder, the notice when a sync pauses, and that `copies.json` is among what to delete there.  For aht's own file copy it covers the list of the receiving folder (and a checksum of the beginning of a file that grew) that aht reads from the other machine before it copies, and the temporary `.aht-partial` folder, with its lock file, that aht makes in the folder it copies into and removes when the copy ends.  It also says that a Windows PC now copies its backups to another machine and fetches them from there.  For Bring Here and Send Back it says what aht reads from the project's home (its list of projects, the chosen project's files, Claude Code's history and plans) and what it tells and writes there, the new fields of `copies.json` (`from_path`, `system`, `autocrlf`) and that this computer now keeps one too for the projects it brings here (`brought`, then `returned`), the home folder, path rule and aht's id of each machine in `config.json`, Claude Code's trust set here for a project brought here, the `.aht-link-…` and `.aht-eol-…` files aht briefly makes, and that a session's git settings come from its environment, never from `.git/config`.

**Unsigned builds.** The app is ad-hoc signed, so macOS blocks its first launch (downloaded or Homebrew-installed alike): allow it once under System Settings > Privacy & Security > Open Anyway, or run `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/aht.app`. Windows SmartScreen shows "unknown publisher" on first run: choose *More info > Run anyway*. The checksums above let you verify what you downloaded.

Every artifact was built and smoke-tested on the matching CI runner before publishing.
